title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
What Is an Orchestrator?
An orchestrator manages when work runs, what depends on what, and how failures are handled.

It connects steps into reliable pipelines
It schedules recurring work and retries failures
It gives you logs, lineage, and a UI for monitoring
It coordinates work, but usually does not do the heavy computation itself

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Popular examples:

Apache Airflow, the original widely adopted workflow orchestrator
Prefect, a simpler and more lightweight alternative for many teams
Dagster, a newer tool that focuses on data assets and developer experience

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Why Python?
Most modern orchestrators are Python-first, but that does not mean your whole workflow must be Python. You can still run R scripts, SQL, shell commands, or containerized tools as steps in an orchestrated pipeline. Think of Python as the “glue” that connects your existing tools into a repeatable, observable workflow.

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Why Dagster for Livestock Research?

Data arrives continuously: sensors, GPS collars, and APIs
Reproducibility is critical for scientific workflows
Asset lineage helps explain how datasets were produced
Schedules and automation reduce manual refresh work
Nice UI for tracing what ran, what failed, and what data changed
Easier to reason about than task-only workflow tools when the output dataset is the real product

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Why Dagster?

Focuses on data assets, not just tasks
Makes dependencies between datasets explicit
Has a clean UI for materializations, lineage, and observability
Plays well with Python, while still letting you call out to R when that is the right tool

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Definitions
Definitions is the top-level Dagster object where you register the pieces of your project.

Assets: what data products exist
Jobs: what can be executed
Schedules: when things should run
Resources: external systems like APIs, databases, or file paths

Dagster uses this registry to understand the shape of the project and to power the UI.

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Asset
A durable data product that Dagster can track over time.
Think of an asset as the thing you actually care about producing, not just the code that made it.
The actual data product could be a CSV, Parquet, or JSON file, a database table, an in-memory data frame, or even a machine learning model.
Dagster records when it was produced, what code produced it, and what it depends on
Examples:

10 Hz Accelerometer data from ear tags stored as an in-memory data frame
GPS points from virtual fence collars written to a table in a database
API data from a GreenFeed machine downloaded to a CSV file

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Job
Jobs are how you run a pipeline in Dagster. A pipeline is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of ops that produce assets.
Use a job when you want a repeatable unit of work, such as a daily download from an API or a full pipeline.
The key to a job is that it is repeatable and deterministic: the same inputs should produce the same outputs.
Jobs can be triggered manually, via a schedule, or via an external event.

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Schedule
A schedule is a time-based trigger that launches a job automatically.
It is how you say, “run this every morning” without manually clicking anything.

title: Dagster Fundamentals for Precision Livestock Technology
text:
Sensor
A sensor is an event-driven trigger that launches a job when an external condition is met.
Instead of running on a clock, a sensor polls for something: a new file, a changed value, or an API returning fresh data.
Examples in livestock research:

A new accelerometer upload appears in a shared folder
A GreenFeed API endpoint returns a record newer than the last ingestion
LoRaWAN gateway reports new data from on-farm sensors

Use a sensor when the data arrives irregularly and a fixed schedule would either miss events or run unnecessarily.
My favorite pattern is to drag and drop a file into a specified folder, and have a sensor detect that file and trigger a job to process it. It’s the lazy scientist’s dream: just drop the file and let the orchestrator handle the rest.

section: How I Use Dagster (My GreenFeed Data Pipeline)
text:
How I Use Dagster (My GreenFeed Data Pipeline)

Download GreenFeed Data API every morning at 3:00 AM MST
Write raw data to CSV file in shared storage
Run R script to clean data (e.g., remove duplicates, standardize column names, drop erroneous values)
Write cleaned data to table in duckdb database
Run R script to enrich cleaned data with contextual metadata (ranch, species, animal class, feed type)
Persist enriched dataset to a second duckdb table for downstream analysis
